title: The One With Rachels Big Kiss

jokes.text: Out of all of us, who do you think will get married next? — Probably Monica and Chandler.
jokes.setup: Someone asks which of their friend group will get married next, as if it's genuinely uncertain.
jokes.punchline: The answer is Monica and Chandler — who are ALREADY engaged. The question is absurd because the answer is blindingly obvious.
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional opener joke. The humor is in the deadpan obviousness of the answer — but it's too mild to register as much more than a throat-clearing gag. No real character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica.

jokes.text: Rachel asks for a pack of Newport Lights in what turns out to be a bookstore or non-tobacco shop; clerk redirects her across the street.
jokes.setup: Rachel walks up to what appears to be a counter and confidently asks for cigarettes.
jokes.punchline: The clerk tells her they don't sell cigarettes — she's in the wrong kind of store entirely, revealing her obliviousness to her surroundings.
jokes.explanation: A mild character beat that establishes Rachel's self-absorbed obliviousness. Functional but forgettable — the punchline isn't surprising enough to land big.

jokes.text: Rachel sees Melissa and mutters to herself: 'I don't think I have the energy for this.'
jokes.setup: Rachel spots an old sorority acquaintance approaching.
jokes.punchline: Her dread is so palpable and honest that it immediately communicates the exhausting nature of forced sorority small talk — a universally relatable feeling.
jokes.explanation: A compact, honest character moment. Rachel's weary aside is relatable and sets up the irony of the overly enthusiastic reunion that follows. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that... Jessica Lockwood from high school?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She's walking this way. Okay, okay, I can do this. Just smile and wave.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, did we actually like each other back then or just... exist in the same hallway?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How much small talk energy do I have left today? I already used it on the barista.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She's getting closer. Do I hug? Do I do the awkward half-wave? Why is this so hard?

jokes.text: Melissa explodes with 'Oh my God! Ray-Ray Greene!' and they scream at each other.
jokes.setup: Rachel's dread is immediately confirmed when Melissa is exactly as exhaustingly enthusiastic as feared.
jokes.punchline: The payoff to Rachel's dread — Melissa is a full-volume sorority tornado, using the nickname 'Ray-Ray.'
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom payoff — the dread joke earns its laugh here. Melissa's energy is a good comedic foil for Rachel. Functional and crowd-pleasing.

dialogue.line: Overly familiar sorority-style nickname

jokes.text: 'You've been MIA for seven sorority newsletters.'
jokes.setup: Melissa is thrilled to see Rachel after a long absence.
jokes.punchline: She measures the absence in 'sorority newsletters' — a hyper-specific metric that perfectly reveals her character and the absurdity of sorority culture.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'seven sorority newsletters' is what makes this work — it's a great character-revealing detail that also mocks sorority culture organically. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: I've been keeping track of everyone who hasn't responded to my newsletter.

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: Rachel - opened it twice, clicked zero links. Monica - marked as spam after issue three. Chandler - unsubscribed, then resubscribed, then unsubscribed again in the same week.

jokes.text: Melissa: 'So last I heard you were gonna get married. Poor Ray-Ray.' Rachel: 'Oh no, it's all good. I actually work at Ralph Lauren.' Melissa: 'Shut up!'
jokes.setup: Melissa pities Rachel for presumably a failed engagement (a low point) and Rachel pivots to her career success.
jokes.punchline: 'Shut up!' as an expression of excited disbelief is both funny in its hyperbole and sets up the running 'shut up' gag with Melissa.
jokes.explanation: Establishes Melissa's over-the-top sorority energy and sets up the running 'shut up' gag. Functional character introduction humor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I got the job at Ralph Lauren!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Shut up!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm serious!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Shut up!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They offered me the position!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Shut up!

jokes.text: Shut up! — I will not. I'm the divisional head of men's sportswear.
jokes.setup: Melissa reacts to Rachel's impressive job title with 'Shut up!' as a compliment.
jokes.punchline: Rachel earnestly refuses — 'I will not' — taking the expression completely literally in a moment of sincere pride.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean play on the colloquial 'shut up' meaning 'no way.' Rachel's literal refusal is a small but charming character moment. Becomes a running joke with Melissa.

dialogue.line: Pushy declaration rather than invitation

jokes.text: Melissa: 'Shut up more! Are you friends with Ralph?' Rachel: 'Oh, please.' Melissa: 'Are you?' Rachel: '...No.'
jokes.setup: Melissa escalates her enthusiasm by assuming Rachel must be personal friends with Ralph Lauren.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'Oh, please' pretends to deflect the question from modesty, but the beat pause and her flat 'No' reveals she was actually hoping to seem like she might be — and she's not.
jokes.explanation: A nicely constructed beat. The comedic structure is tight: faux-modesty deflection → beat → honest admission. Very character-specific to Rachel's vanity and insecurity. The 'Oh, please' reads as humility before the punchline deflates her completely.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I really want to help people and make a difference in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm a party planner.

jokes.text: Melissa hands Rachel a card and says she got out of real estate to 'help people and make a difference.' Rachel asks what she does now. Melissa: 'I'm a party planner.'
jokes.setup: Melissa builds up the reveal of her new career with grandiose language about helping people and making a difference.
jokes.punchline: She's a party planner — the total deflation of the noble framing.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom misdirection with solid structure. The pomposity of 'help people and make a difference' is perfectly engineered for a deflating punchline. Good economy and a reliably funny beat type.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hey Phi Phi!

jokes.text: Joey, unable to contain himself: 'They were lovers.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are circling around what Rachel and her college friend 'did,' using vague pronouns and knowing looks, drawing it out.
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts through all the delicate tiptoeing with two blunt words: 'They were lovers.' Delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's total lack of social filter combined with the absurd formality of 'lovers' (rather than any cruder or more casual term) is perfectly him. The economy is exceptional — two words do what a paragraph of dancing-around couldn't. Highly character-specific and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. What were you gonna say about Rachel and Melissa? Come on, don't leave me hanging!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Seriously, you can't just cut off like that. What happened between them?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm begging you. Just tell me. Please?

jokes.text: After Rachel explains the kiss, Chandler deadpans: 'So that's two of my wives.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just revealed she kissed Melissa in college. The group is processing this.
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually notes this makes two of his 'wives' (Monica and Rachel, since Rachel was briefly married to Ross — who is Chandler's friend group) who have kissed women, delivered with complete deadpan resignation.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — Chandler's deadpan self-pity is perfectly in character. The 'my wives' construction is unexpected and mines the show's history (Ross and Rachel's Vegas wedding, Monica being his actual fiancée). The resigned 'two of my wives' implies a comically expanding universe of his marital connections. Highly quotable and very Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I cannot believe you two went to summer camp together and never told me this! Do you understand what this means? You're basically sisters. No, you're better than sisters. You're camp sisters. And camp sisters are forever. This changes everything. Everything!

jokes.text: Rachel looks at the seating chart and suggests Monica just put her pin 'with a Manhattan in my hand, talking to the cute bartender.'
jokes.setup: Monica is using a physical seating chart with pins to plan her wedding. She finds Rachel's pin and places it.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately redirects her pin placement to illustrate her ideal wedding experience — not at any table, but at the bar hitting on the bartender — revealing her priorities.
jokes.explanation: A character-specific moment that plays on Rachel's flirtatious, self-centered nature. Amusing but not exceptional — the joke type is well-worn for her character.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. Rachel kissed a woman?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, her name was Melissa.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God! Emily kissed a woman!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Carol kissed a woman!

jokes.text: Joey (pointing at the seating chart pins): 'These pins aren't for playing, are they?'
jokes.setup: Monica is using a formal wedding seating chart with colored pins. Joey is clearly eyeing them.
jokes.punchline: Joey has apparently been contemplating playing with the pins like toys, only asking for permission now — revealing his childlike impulses.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean Joey character beat. His childlike curiosity and the slight embarrassment of having to ask is well-captured. Economy is good; character-specific, though not especially novel for Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, Rachel, you're sitting at table seven.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, who else is at table seven?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Um, some cousins, Uncle Frank, and that guy Derek from my yoga class.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Derek? Derek with the amazing arms? Oh my God, Monica, I'm going to be so charming. I'm gonna flip my hair, I'm gonna laugh at all his jokes, even the stupid ones. He's gonna think I'm so cool and sophisticated, and then maybe he'll ask me to dance, and then we'll fall in love, get married, and have beautiful babies named Derek Jr. and Little Bella!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, he's gay.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Joey complains he only has 10 blue pins. Monica says 'it's not a contest.' Chandler: 'Certainly not a close one.'
jokes.setup: Joey laments his small number of invited guests (10 blue pins). Monica tries to be diplomatic.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's immediate, flat agreement that it's definitely NOT a close contest undercuts Monica's diplomatic effort and twists the knife on Joey.
jokes.explanation: A crisply executed Chandler one-liner. He validates Monica's lie while simultaneously destroying it, landing a dry stab at Joey. Good structure — the callback to 'contest' gives it a slight setup/punchline architecture. Economical and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hey, it's okay. A lot of people couldn't make it. It doesn't mean anything.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, look at it this way — you're marrying me. That's what matters.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, not really. You have no friends.

jokes.text: Joey stares at Rachel after learning she kissed a woman. Rachel notices: 'Stop picturing it!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just disclosed kissing Melissa. Joey is now in the room and clearly visualizing the scene.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's command 'Stop picturing it!' confirms she can read exactly what's on Joey's face without him saying a word — and the audience sees his caught-out expression.
jokes.explanation: A reliable but well-executed visual comedy beat. Joey's reaction face does the work; Rachel's line is the perfect acknowledgment. Very character-specific — no other character would be so transparently imagining it. Gets a solid audience laugh from the studio crowd.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? I'm not... I didn't... Ross!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Stop doing that!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Doing what?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That! With your eyes! You're doing it right now!

jokes.text: Joey suggests they invite his parents. Monica: 'Your parents are coming. Chandler's are coming. Ross' parents are coming.' Joey: 'Ross' parents are my parents.'
jokes.setup: Monica explains why Joey's suggestion is redundant — she lists whose parents are coming.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he considers the Gellers to be his parents too — a sweetly delusional claim that shows how thoroughly he's absorbed himself into the friend group as family.
jokes.explanation: A charming character beat that reveals the depth of Joey's bond with the group while also being slightly delusional-absurd. Character-specific and emotionally warm underneath the joke. Works well.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where are my parents going to sit?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, well, they're not invited.

jokes.text: Joey, after Monica agrees to try fitting in more people: 'You just want more blue pins.'
jokes.setup: Monica appears to be generously accommodating Joey by rearranging the seating chart.
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts through her altruism and correctly identifies her real motivation: she wants more blue (her) pins to outnumber his red ones — proving it IS a contest.
jokes.explanation: A callback to the pin contest running gag. Joey's moment of unexpected perceptiveness is funny because it subverts his usual obliviousness. Nicely ties a bow on the pins subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, parents always show up for their kids' big moments!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey... we're siblings. We have the same parents.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Monica, solving the seating problem: 'Rachel may have to sit at the bar.' Rachel: 'That is not a problem.'
jokes.setup: Monica needs to rearrange seating and suggests Rachel's pin goes to the bar.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's immediate, enthusiastic confirmation that this is fine — directly echoing her earlier fantasy about hanging at the bar — works as a callback to joke #9.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that pays off the earlier bar joke. The structure is clean and Monica's slightly exasperated delivery makes it land. Good economy in Rachel's reply.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We should invite my parents over for dinner!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, your mom makes that amazing lasagna, doesn't she?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, the best!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So that's what this is about.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Maybe you'll order a little sangria.' Rachel: 'Get out of here!'
jokes.setup: Monica is riffing on the seating solution while also slyly referencing the sangria-and-kissing story Rachel just told.
jokes.punchline: The 'sangria' reference is a double callback — to Rachel's story about getting drunk on sangria and kissing Melissa, AND to Melissa's catchphrase 'shut up.' Rachel's irritated 'Get out of here!' mirrors the 'shut up' energy.
jokes.explanation: A layered callback that rewards attentive viewers. Monica's teasing is sharp and the 'Get out of here!' reply is a nice mirror to Melissa's 'shut up.' Shows good writers-room craft in threading references.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, maybe you could sit at the bar.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: At the bar? Why would I sit at the bar?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't know, you could have a Cosmopolitan... the drink, not the magazine.

jokes.text: Rachel tells the tuxedo shop owner she's Monica's maid of honor and can't be invited as a guest. Owner: 'Okay, don't try to blue-pin me.'
jokes.setup: The owner is offering tuxes and says he wants to attend the wedding as Monica's guest. Rachel points out she's the maid of honor.
jokes.punchline: The owner has somehow already absorbed the 'blue pin' metaphor from the seating chart subplot — a quick, absurdist callback that's also self-referential in a fun way.
jokes.explanation: A fun meta callback that extends the pin gag to a new character unexpectedly. Slightly strained — the owner knowing this term requires the audience to accept a small logical stretch — but it's endearing and quick.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're trying to steal me for your guest count!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not stealing you. I'm just saying it would be really great if you came.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, you have a plus-one. Use it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but you're way more fun than a plus-one.

jokes.text: Ross is excited about celebrity tuxedos: 'They've been down the red carpet with people yelling... Who are you wearing? You look fabulous!'
jokes.setup: The shop owner explains that the tuxedos were worn by celebrities.
jokes.punchline: Ross's excited re-enactment of red carpet commentary — delivered with slightly too much enthusiasm — characterizes his nerdish excitement over pop culture proximity.
jokes.explanation: A mild character moment. Ross's slightly uncool enthusiasm is on-brand but the joke itself is thin — it's more setup for the ESPN joke that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! What's with all the excitement? Did they finally cancel Baywatch?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I got invited to walk the red carpet at the Golden Globes!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The Golden Globes? That's great! Now you can stand next to beautiful women and feel bad about yourself in person instead of just on TV.

jokes.text: Shop owner to Ross: 'Might I suggest watching a little more ESPN and a little less E!'
jokes.setup: Ross has just enthusiastically recreated red carpet commentary ('Who are you wearing? You look fabulous!'), displaying an un-masculine knowledge of celebrity fashion coverage.
jokes.punchline: The owner's gentle suggestion to watch ESPN instead of E! is a polite but clear implication that Ross is not masculine enough in his entertainment choices.
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured joke. The ESPN/E! binary is an efficient shorthand for the masculinity joke. The shop owner's deadpan delivery elevates it. Becomes a running thread through the episode (ESPN callbacks).

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you have to know who Paul O'Neill is. He's only like the greatest right fielder in baseball history.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, maybe you should watch ESPN or something.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler's right. You really should.

jokes.text: Shop owner: 'This one is Paul O'Neil.' Chandler: 'Who's that?' Owner: 'He plays for the Yankees. Seriously, ESPN.'
jokes.setup: Owner is showing off celebrity-worn tuxedos. He names Paul O'Neil.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, supposedly the more masculine counterpart to Ross, also doesn't know who Paul O'Neil is — triggering the ESPN callback again.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the ESPN running gag. The joke is funnier the second time because now BOTH men are indicted. Chandler's ignorance about a Yankees player (while living in New York) is a nice specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm wearing Pierce Brosnan's tux? Oh my God, oh my God! I'm James Bond. I'm actually James Bond.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The name's Geller. Ross Geller.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have a license to kill... And I'm going to use it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Shaken, not stirred. That's what I always say. Except I've never been shaken or stirred. But now I will be.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I drive an Aston Martin. I have a tiny jet-pack. Women throw themselves at me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm sophisticated. I'm worldly. I'm... I'm everything I've ever wanted to be.

jokes.text: Ross learns the tux was worn by Pierce Brosnan — James Bond — and completely loses his mind: 'I would be England's most powerful weapon. A jet-setting heartbreaker on Her Majesty's secret service. A man who fears no one, with a license to kill.'
jokes.setup: The shop owner reveals a tux was worn by Pierce Brosnan. Ross connects this to James Bond.
jokes.punchline: Ross goes on an increasingly grandiose fantasy about being James Bond, culminating in 'a license to kill' — before immediately deflating with 'Would Monica let me wear this?'
jokes.explanation: A strong character escalation. Ross's fantasy builds beautifully from 'cool tux' to 'license to kill' and then is immediately punctured by his Monica-fear. The deflation is perfectly timed and deeply character-specific — the contrast between his self-image and his reality is Ross's core comedic essence. The final 'Would Monica let me wear this?' is the punchline that makes it sing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm like James Bond. I can do whatever I want, whenever I want.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You need to ask me first.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right. Can I do whatever I want, whenever I want?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: 'Would Monica let me wear this?' — Ross's immediate deflation after his Bond fantasy.
jokes.setup: Ross has just delivered an escalating fantasy about being James Bond — 'a man who fears no one, with a license to kill.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks if Monica would let him wear it, undercutting his entire Bond fantasy with the reality of his relationship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: This is the punchline to joke #21 and deserves its own entry as the payoff beat. The escalation from 'license to kill' to 'would Monica let me' is a near-perfect comedic inversion. Ross's henpecked reality demolishes his grandiose self-image in one breath. Character integration is exceptional — this only works because of the established Monica/Ross friend dynamic. Economy is superb: five words do enormous work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what are you wearing to the wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm wearing my grandmother's wedding dress. Well, half of it anyway. The other half is a lovely piece of a shower curtain I found.

jokes.text: Joey and Phoebe are playing chess, apparently in their own idiosyncratic way. Joey: 'Chess!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe says 'We should really learn how to play the real way. I like our way.' Then Joey exclaims 'Chess!' as if making a move.
jokes.punchline: The implication is that their version of chess involves yelling the word 'Chess!' instead of 'Check' — or possibly some entirely different game they've invented and called chess.
jokes.explanation: A charming absurdist bit. Joey and Phoebe's parallel idiocy playing 'their version' of chess, plus his triumphant 'Chess!' (presumably instead of 'check' or 'checkmate'), is a simple but effective visual gag. Very character-specific to these two. The brevity is a strength.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Can I come to your dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, no. It's just going to be me and my girlfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh come on, I promise I'll be good. I just want to meet her.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, the last time you said that, you tried to hide a camera in the centerpiece.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was one time! And in my defense, I was going to donate the footage to science.

jokes.text: Joey says he's not wearing a tux — he's going to wear 'multi-colored robes. And maybe a hat.'
jokes.setup: The shop owner has set aside tuxedos for Chandler and Ross. He asks Joey if he needs one.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he's planning to officiate the wedding in multi-colored robes and possibly a hat — a completely unexpected and chaotic costume choice for a solemn occasion.
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious ambition to jazz up the wedding ceremony with flamboyant minister attire is a solid character joke. 'And maybe a hat' is the right beat to add — the casual afterthought of the hat is what makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I kissed her!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes, I did!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: When?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: At Carol's birthday party!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was at Carol's birthday party, and I did not see that.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Does Monica know about this?' Joey: 'No.' Ross: 'Can I please be there when you tell her?'
jokes.setup: Joey reveals Monica doesn't know about his robe-and-hat plan for the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately asks to witness the conversation — implying Monica's reaction will be spectacular and that he wants a front-row seat to the chaos.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean callback to Monica's controlling nature. Ross's eagerness to witness the confrontation is a nice character touch — he's not protecting Joey, he's relishing the inevitability. Economical and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that sounds nice. But in my experience, that's just what people say when they've been making out for like twenty minutes and they need to come up for air.

jokes.text: Rachel explains that she and Melissa kissed. Phoebe, flatly: 'Yeah, I'm sure that happened.'
jokes.setup: Rachel earnestly insists on the truth of her college kiss story.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's completely flat, dismissive 'Yeah, I'm sure that happened' establishes the disbelief running gag that drives the B-plot.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's skepticism is perfectly flat and economical. It sets up the episode's running joke about no one believing Rachel while also being funny on its own. Phoebe's deadpan is usually reserved for more whimsical disbelief — here it works for dismissive irony too.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I just don't believe you, Rachel. You've never done anything wild in your entire life.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? That's not true! I have done wild things!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Name one.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I... well, there was that time in Cancun...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You went to Cancun with your parents.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. But please, Phoebe, you have to let me have this one thing. This is my one wild story. Don't take it away from me!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Okay. I just didn't know that you were a lesbian.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been defending her story and insisting the kiss happened. Phoebe is trying to understand Rachel's sexuality.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually labels Rachel a lesbian as if that's the only logical conclusion — missing the nuance entirely and reducing the whole thing to a simple binary in classic Phoebe fashion.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's oblivious reductionism is classic. The joke is in her earnestness — she's not being mean, she just sees the world in very simple terms. Character-specific and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It did happen! We kissed!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. So if you kissed, then you must be married. That's how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? No, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious. Kiss equals marriage. It's science.

jokes.text: Phoebe calls Rachel 'vanilla.' Rachel: 'Vanilla? I'm not vanilla. I do lots of crazy things. I mean, I got drunk and married in Vegas.' Phoebe: 'To Ross.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls Rachel 'vanilla' (boring/safe) and Rachel tries to defend her wild-side credentials with her most extreme example.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's two-word response — 'To Ross' — is the perfect deflation, implying that marrying Ross is so anti-exciting that it cancels out the wildness of the Vegas wedding entirely.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The 'To Ross' punchline is devastating in its economy — two words that simultaneously burn Ross, validate Phoebe's vanilla argument, and play on the show's history. The structure is excellent: Rachel sets up her best evidence, Phoebe dismantles it in two words. Highly quotable. The joke only works because of deep character and show history integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not vanilla! I did something crazy once. I married my ex-husband.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Okay. Because I can't picture it.' Rachel: 'You should get inside my head.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe agrees to come to dinner to get Melissa to confirm the story, but admits she can't visualize Rachel kissing a woman.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'You should get inside my head' is both a callback to Joey's visualizing gag AND an ironic self-awareness that she's been picturing it herself.
jokes.explanation: A decent callback that works on two levels — Rachel acknowledging both Phoebe's inability to picture it and her own investment in the story. Slightly less sharp than the jokes around it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I can picture it.

jokes.text: Joey guesses Chandler has a 'freakishly thin date with a hanger for a head' as his wedding gift.
jokes.setup: Joey asks Chandler to guess what he got for the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Joey's guess is surreally specific — a 'freakishly thin date with a hanger for a head' — a bizarrely vivid image that reveals more about Joey's imagination than anything else.
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly vivid and strange insult from Joey that works because of its specificity. 'A hanger for a head' is a memorably weird image. The joke is funnier for being delivered as a sincere guess rather than an intentional burn.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Guess what I got!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, a girlfriend? That's amazing! Wait, no... a gym membership? No, that's not it either. Oh! I know! You finally got rid of that awful bracelet!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, whatever it is, it's probably going to disappoint me less than your last three relationships.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Batman's tux! Made expressly for Val Kilmer, and worn by him in the hit film... that Batman film he was in.'
jokes.setup: Joey is building up the reveal of a tuxedo worn by Val Kilmer in Batman.
jokes.punchline: The trailing-off into '...that Batman film he was in' is funny because Joey clearly doesn't know the actual title of the movie, puncturing his dramatic build-up.
jokes.explanation: A nice Joey moment. The dramatic build-up collapses into the vague 'that Batman film he was in' — perfectly capturing Joey's broad showmanship masking total ignorance. Specific, character-integrated, and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more Batman? I mean, I'm dark, I'm mysterious, I work alone...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What movie is that from?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have no idea.

jokes.text: Ross tells Joey he can't wear the Val Kilmer tux: 'If you wear that, it'll make mine less special.'
jokes.setup: Ross is wearing James Bond's tux. Joey has obtained Batman's tux and wants to wear it too.
jokes.punchline: Ross's reasoning — that Joey wearing a cool tux diminishes the specialness of his cool tux — is simultaneously petty and completely logical, revealing Ross's competitive insecurity.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat that plays on Ross's low-key pettiness and need to feel special. The logic is funny because it's correct within Ross's worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I promise to love you, to cherish you, to be there for you, in sickness and in health, for richer or poorer, till death do us part.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I... uh... yeah... I mean... could I BE any more... married?

jokes.text: Joey to Ross: 'You need something to make it special? You have the most special thing of all. You are marrying the woman you love.'
jokes.setup: Ross is complaining that Joey's cool tux will diminish his own.
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers a genuinely heartfelt, sincere speech about love being the most special thing — which is funny because it's completely earnest, comes from Joey, and also completely sidesteps Ross's petty tux competition.
jokes.explanation: Joey's unexpected wisdom and sincerity is a staple Friends joke type. The humor is in the contrast: Joey's usually selfish/oblivious nature making a genuinely good point. It's character-specific to Joey's sweet-dumb duality.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Chandler, please, I'm begging you. I need the Batman tuxedo for my date.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, that's the least manly thing I've ever heard. You're literally begging for a Batman costume.

jokes.text: Ross caves and says 'Pretty please?' Joey: '"Pretty please?" Not very 007.'
jokes.setup: Ross, trying to persuade Joey not to wear Batman's tux, resorts to 'Pretty please?'
jokes.punchline: Joey points out that 'pretty please' is at odds with Ross's self-image as James Bond — a perfect callback to the Bond fantasy that deflates Ross again.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback joke. 'Not very 007' is perfectly economical and ties back to Ross's earlier fantasy while highlighting the gap between his Bond self-image and his actual 'pretty please' reality. Well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe you did that.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh come on, at least I'm not running around like James Bond with a different woman every week.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, that was a phase!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A phase? Chandler, that was like twelve years.

jokes.text: Joey: 'If you were getting married, I'd never do anything to upset you.' Ross: 'You slept with my sister.' Joey: 'That was pretty 007.'
jokes.setup: Joey promises he would never upset Ross on his wedding day. Ross immediately counters with a devastating factual example.
jokes.punchline: Joey reframes sleeping with Ross's sister as a James Bond-style move — coolly justifying it while also completing the 007 running gag.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The three-beat structure is perfect: Joey's sincere promise → Ross's devastating counter-example → Joey's confident reframe as 007 behavior. The 007 callback is precisely deployed; the dark acknowledgment of sleeping with Ross's sister is both a show-history callback and a character reveal (Joey feels NO remorse). The economy is excellent — 'That was pretty 007' does enormous comedic work. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Your feelings aren't wrong. You're not wanted here.

jokes.text: Joey tells Monica his parents think she only invited them because of him. Monica: 'That's too bad. It's true. But too bad.'
jokes.setup: Joey reports that his parents feel unwanted and think they were only invited as a courtesy.
jokes.punchline: Monica's response is disarmingly honest — she confirms their suspicion is correct — but sandwiches it between two 'too bad's that show she still doesn't care.
jokes.explanation: Monica's blunt honesty wrapped in social niceties is a perfect character moment. 'That's too bad. It's true. But too bad.' is a beautiful three-part construction — the acknowledgment of truth sandwiched between dismissals is very Monica. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Your mother hasn't sent lasagnas in weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, maybe she's busy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, she sends them every week. What happened to them?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay... they were just so good, and they were sitting there...

jokes.text: Joey guilts Monica: 'This is a woman who has sent you many lasagnas.' Monica: 'No, she hasn't.' Joey: 'Is it her fault if some didn't make it to you?'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to guilt Monica into calling his mother by citing her supposed generosity.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately denies receiving any lasagnas; Joey's baffling counter — implying the lasagnas existed but were intercepted somehow — is wonderfully absurd and reveals he may have eaten them himself.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully absurd Joey moment. The implication that the lasagnas existed but 'didn't make it' is delightfully vague — was he eating them? Did they get lost? The fact that he doesn't explain makes it funnier. 'Is it her fault if some didn't make it to you?' is a genuinely great line. Character-specific and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's not my fault! The postal service lost it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you didn't even mail it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if the postal service wasn't run by... you know... *those people*...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying... actually, no, wait. My mailman is great. Never mind.

jokes.text: Joey: 'They hate the post office. And the Irish. But I don't think you could blame it on them.'
jokes.setup: Joey is suggesting Monica blame the missing invitations on the post office. He adds detail about his family's grudges.
jokes.punchline: The completely unexpected addition of 'and the Irish' as a secondary Tribbianni family grievance — delivered as a helpful clarification — is a brilliantly absurd character detail.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully specific, absurdist family detail. The Tribbianis hating the Irish is funny precisely because it's so random and Joey delivers it as pure practical information. The addition 'but I don't think you could blame it on them' (the Irish) makes it even better — he's being helpful. Very quotable and genuinely original.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe how slow the postal service is. I mailed that package two weeks ago and it still hasn't arrived!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, those postal workers are all lazy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right. Those postal workers ARE all lazy!

jokes.text: Monica on the phone with Joey's mom, covering for the late invitation: 'I guess there was some screw-up at the damn post office.' Joey's mom apparently commiserates. Monica: 'Yeah, the U.S. Post Office? No. More like U.S. Lost Office.'
jokes.setup: Monica has been drafted against her will to call Joey's mom and blame the post office for the invitation snafu.
jokes.punchline: Monica gets so into the bit that she starts making post-office jokes with Joey's mom — riffing on 'U.S. Lost Office' — completely abandoning her reluctance and getting competitive about hating the post office.
jokes.explanation: Monica's transformation from reluctant liar to enthusiastic post-office ranter is a good character beat. 'U.S. Lost Office' is a weak pun but the character behavior drives the laugh more than the wordplay.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I was in a sorority. Delta Nu Theta.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound right.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, they were very selective. You had to have done it with at least two teachers.

jokes.text: Rachel asks Melissa if she was in a sorority. Melissa: 'Of course. Yes. I was a Thigh Mega Tampon.'
jokes.setup: Melissa is describing Allen's fraternity at Syracuse, and Rachel asks if she was in a sorority too.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe invents the fictional sorority 'Thigh Mega Tampon' — a crude pun on Greek-letter sorority names — and delivers it with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Wait — context suggests this is actually Phoebe at the dinner with Melissa, not Rachel. 'Thigh Mega Tampon' is a brilliantly absurd fake sorority name — the kind of inspired nonsense that is pure Phoebe. The confidence of delivery makes it funnier. It's crude but clever. Very quotable and genuinely original.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My sorority sisters and I used to go to this bar, but then there was this incident with the fire and the peacock, and we all had to change our identities. That's why I'm Phoebe now. My real name is Regina Phalange.

jokes.text: Melissa: 'What one?' Phoebe: 'We were huge too. But they had to shut us down when Regina Phalangie died of alcohol poisoning.'
jokes.setup: Melissa (unfamiliar with Phoebe) takes the bait on 'Thigh Mega Tampon' and asks for more details.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe elaborates with an entirely fictional backstory involving 'Regina Phalangie' (one of Phoebe's recurring aliases) dying of alcohol poisoning — completely fabricated and delivered with earnest sadness.
jokes.explanation: Regina Phalangie is one of Phoebe's recurring fake aliases in the Friends universe, making this a meta-callback for dedicated viewers. The earnest elaboration of a completely fabricated sorority tragedy, delivered with Phoebe's characteristic sincere sadness, is a strong character moment. Good structure — the follow-up question gives Phoebe room to deepen the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My grandmother actually died of alcohol poisoning.

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: Cool!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Isn't it a shame when one girl ruins it for the whole bunch?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just explained that her (fictional) sorority was shut down due to Regina Phalangie's alcohol poisoning death.
jokes.punchline: The philosophical moral Phoebe draws from the tragedy — 'isn't it a shame when one girl ruins it for the whole bunch' — treats the death as merely a logistical inconvenience, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A dark-subversive button on the sorority story. Phoebe's breezy moral lesson about a fictional alcohol poisoning death is funny because of how completely it misses the gravity of death. Very Phoebe — she applies clichéd wisdom to inappropriate situations. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Melissa, remember when we went to that coffee place?

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: Um, no?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know, the one with the chairs? And the... coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I don't remember.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How could you forget? You were wearing that blue sweater. Well, it might have been purple. And you ordered that drink with the foam on top that looked like a little hat?

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: Rachel, I don't think—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And the barista! He had that one eye that was slightly higher than the other eye. And he kept humming that song. You know the one. It went dun-dun-dun-dun-dun?

jokes.text: Melissa: 'Speaking of drinking too much, I told Phoebe... about that crazy night after the Sigma Chi luau where we made out.' Then she describes the coconut bikini tops, etc. Rachel: 'Wow, Ray-Ray, I have no idea what you're talking about.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has brought Phoebe to dinner specifically to get Melissa to confirm the kissing story. Melissa freely brings it up herself.
jokes.punchline: In a complete reversal, Melissa now denies the kiss — claiming to have 'no idea' what Rachel is talking about — after Rachel spent the whole episode fighting to prove it happened.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural reversal. The irony is well-executed — Rachel brought Melissa to prove her point, but Melissa's denial is the punchline to the whole episode setup. The timing is good, though the reason for the denial (Melissa is in love with Rachel, revealed later) recontextualizes it on rewatch. Strong structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I remember it exactly like this...

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: That's not what happened at all.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes it was!

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: No, it wasn't.

jokes.text: Ross walks in wearing the tux. Joey: 'Ross is Batman.' Monica: 'Well, he did manage to keep his identity secret for a long time.'
jokes.setup: Ross is wearing the Val Kilmer/Batman tux. Joey announces 'Ross is Batman.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry response — that Ross 'managed to keep his identity secret for a long time' — is an ambiguous burn that could refer to Bruce Wayne hiding his Batman identity OR to some other secret Ross has been keeping (possibly about his sexuality or other quirks).
jokes.explanation: Monica's line works as both a Batman reference AND a dig at Ross — the double meaning is what elevates it. The ambiguity is productive comedy. Well-structured and character-specific to Monica's sharp, dry wit.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'm Wonder Woman. I just don't tell anyone.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Well, he did manage to keep his identity secret for a long time.'
jokes.setup: Joey says 'Ross is Batman.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's response implies Ross is secretly more interesting than people think — a mild joke that also plays on Ross's general uninteresting reputation.
jokes.explanation: A quick follow-up joke that extends the Batman visual gag. Phoebe's reading of Batman-as-secret-identity playing off Ross's perceived dullness is a fun beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: James Bond gets all the ladies. Batman? Not so much.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I mean, think about it. Bond has Pussy Galore, Vesper Lynd... Batman's got Robin.

jokes.text: Ross: '007 has all those gadgets.' Chandler: 'Batman has a utility belt.' Ross: '007 has a fancy car.' Chandler: 'Batman has the Batmobile.' Ross: '007 gets all the ladies.' Chandler: 'Batman has Robin.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler debate whether James Bond or Batman is cooler, using alternating categories.
jokes.punchline: The escalating exchange culminates in Ross arguing 007 'gets all the ladies' — to which Chandler counters 'Batman has Robin.' The implication (Robin as Bond's equivalent to 'the ladies') is an elegantly understated joke.
jokes.explanation: A finely structured escalating debate. Each exchange is a mini-setup/punchline, but the final 'Batman has Robin' as the equivalent of Bond's women is the best beat — it's understated, slightly transgressive, and perfectly economical. The structure is tight and the escalation is well-paced. Gets a big laugh in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We have a martini, shaken not stirred, just like James Bond.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Do you have chocolate milk?

jokes.text: Beat after 'Batman has Robin.' Chandler and Ross pause. Chandler: 'We get ESPN, right?'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just implied something about Batman and Robin's relationship. Both men process this for a beat.
jokes.punchline: Chandler breaks the silence by anxiously checking that they get ESPN — reverting to the masculine validation running gag from the tuxedo shop, implying he's concerned about what his Robin comment revealed.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed reaction beat. The silence after 'Batman has Robin' is the setup; Chandler's anxious ESPN question is the perfect callback punchline. It wraps two running gags together (ESPN + Batman/Bond debate) in four words. The economy is superb. The timing depends on the actors holding the beat — a rewatch reward.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is gonna be the best show!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, it's a wedding, not a show.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right, right... the best wedding show!

jokes.text: Monica offers to put Ross in the Bond mood: 'How about you go put on your 007 tuxedo, and I'll make you a martini?' Ross: 'I don't like martinis.' Monica: 'A Yoo-Hoo with a funny straw?' Ross: 'Yum.'
jokes.setup: Monica tries to play along with Ross's Bond fantasy by offering a martini.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately breaks the fantasy by admitting he doesn't like martinis; Monica immediately offers 'A Yoo-Hoo with a funny straw' — a child's drink — and Ross enthusiastically accepts.
jokes.explanation: An excellent three-beat gag. Monica sets up the Bond world → Ross immediately shatters it → Monica perfectly pivots to something Ross-appropriate. 'Yoo-Hoo with a funny straw' is a great specific detail (Yoo-Hoo is a chocolate milk drink associated with children). Ross's enthusiastic 'Yum' is the perfect button. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't do Tuesday. I've got an audition.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wednesday I'm on stand-by for a callback.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Thursday there's a table read.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And Friday... I'm between projects.

jokes.text: Joey, oblivious to the wedding formality: 'I know the invitation says 6 p.m. But does that mean get there at 6, or the show starts at 6?'
jokes.setup: Monica is discussing wedding logistics with Joey, the officiant.
jokes.punchline: Joey treats the wedding like a theater show — asking about 'doors open' vs. 'curtain up' timing — revealing his entire mental framework is filtered through his entertainment industry experience.
jokes.explanation: A good character beat. Joey's entertainment-industry framing of a wedding ('the show starts at 6') is entirely consistent with how he processes the world. Character integration is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm a professional officiant. I've married... like, a lot of people. I'm basically a marriager.

jokes.text: Joey calls the wedding 'the show,' catches himself, and corrects: 'Right, the wedding. Gotcha.'
jokes.setup: Joey has accidentally referred to the wedding as 'the show.'
jokes.punchline: His self-correction ('Right, the wedding. Gotcha.') with the knowing 'Gotcha' implies he's filed this away but doesn't quite internalize why it matters.
jokes.explanation: A quick follow-through beat. Joey's 'Gotcha' is the right note — he thinks he's learned the right word but hasn't internalized any meaning behind it. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How can I not remember kissing him?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you were pretty drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I wasn't THAT drunk!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rachel, you threw up in my shoe.

jokes.text: Joey: 'But weddings start a little late, right?' Monica: 'Have you ever been to one of my weddings?'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to negotiate the start time so he can attend his niece's christening first.
jokes.punchline: Monica's rhetorical question — 'Have you ever been to one of my weddings?' — is a dry self-reference implying she runs a tight, punctual ship and Joey should know this by now.
jokes.explanation: Monica's line is sharp and character-specific. The implied OCD-precision of her wedding planning is well-established, and 'Have you ever been to one of my weddings?' carries that weight efficiently. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He was very tall, and he had this really nice smile, and these blue eyes...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that sounds like Joey!

jokes.text: Joey: 'My part's in the beginning. I'm not in the rest of the... show. Wedding.'
jokes.setup: Joey is explaining his scheduling conflict — his part is at the beginning of the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: He catches himself saying 'show' again, corrects to 'wedding' — but the fact that he keeps calling it 'the show' reveals the correction from before didn't stick at all.
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the 'show' gag. The rule of three applies — this is the last deployment and the laugh comes from the fact that he just corrected himself and already forgot. Running gags need to escalate; this one stays flat but is still functional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. Maybe it didn't happen. But if it did, that would be sexual assault, and you'd be going to jail.

jokes.text: Joey proposes to 'vamp' until guests arrive — 'warm up the crowd, ask where they're from.' Monica repeats: 'You'll vamp?' Joey: 'Like warm up the crowd. Ask where they're from. In Joey Tribbianni, you get a minister and an entertainer.' He dubs himself a 'ministainer.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to sell Monica on the idea of him stalling the wedding ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Joey invents the portmanteau 'ministainer' (minister + entertainer) and declares himself the best in the business — treating the sacred role of wedding officiant as a Vegas warm-up act.
jokes.explanation: A strong character joke. 'Ministainer' is a great neologism — the kind of word-invention that feels exactly right for Joey. His confidence that there's 'no one better, no one greater' as a minister-entertainer is perfectly oblivious. The word itself is quotable and the character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why are you carrying that invitation around?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Because I'm going to give it to someone.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that narrows it down to like, what, three people?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey!

jokes.text: Joey, in full showman mode: 'There's no one better. There's no one greater.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just coined 'ministainer' and is now delivering his pitch.
jokes.punchline: The rhyming couplet 'no one better / no one greater' sounds like a hip-hop hype lyric or a stadium sports chant being applied to wedding officiating — the incongruity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A secondary beat following the stronger 'ministainer' joke. The rhyming self-aggrandizement is funny but less novel on its own. Part of the same joke unit as #54.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could those pants BE any tighter?

jokes.text: Rachel: 'How can you not remember us kissing?' Melissa: 'I don't know. I don't remember a lot of things that never happened.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is pushing Melissa to confirm the kiss story in front of Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Melissa's response — 'I don't remember a lot of things that never happened' — is a brilliantly cutting non-sequitur that denies the event while also being a perfectly logical statement.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'I don't remember a lot of things that never happened' is a perfectly paradoxical statement — logically tautological but devastatingly dismissive. It's genuinely clever wordplay in service of character. Economical, quotable, and funny on its own as a philosophy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and wit.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm Batman.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This jacket is really uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm... actually quite warm and cozy.

jokes.text: Rachel describes the 'sleeping porch' and coconut bikini tops, then: 'Our coconuts kept knocking together.' Beat. 'Somewhere Joey's head is exploding.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is re-describing the kissing scene to trigger Melissa's memory, including the detail of coconut bikini tops.
jokes.punchline: Rachel (or Phoebe) acknowledges the inherent absurdity of the coconuts detail by imagining Joey's reaction to it — a meta-moment that steps outside the scene to reference a character who isn't there.
jokes.explanation: A smart meta-joke that acknowledges Joey's presence in the audience's imagination. The 'knocking coconuts' detail is already funny; the acknowledgment that Joey would be losing his mind is a great bonus beat. The absent-character callback is a clever structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm wearing a tux from a blind guy movie. Although, I guess that explains the superpowers I've been developing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What superpowers?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The ability to make any woman lose her sight... when she looks at me.

jokes.text: Melissa: 'I'm sorry. I mean, if I thought it happened, I would say it.' Rachel: 'Maybe I passed out and you did stuff to me while I was sleeping.'
jokes.setup: Melissa refuses to confirm the kiss. Rachel is becoming increasingly desperate.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's escalation to 'maybe you did stuff to me while I was sleeping' is a wild swing — she's so committed to the story that she's now willing to entertain a much darker scenario just to have it confirmed.
jokes.explanation: A dark-escalation joke that shows Rachel's desperation reaching absurd lengths. The escalation to a darker scenario for the sake of validation is funny but slightly uncomfortable. The setup is good; the punchline is a bit awkward in its implications.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Fine! You know what? I don't care anymore. You want to get married in a sewage treatment plant? Go ahead!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You want Chandler to wear a dress? I don't care!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You want to have Janice as a bridesmaid? Fine!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'It's okay, you don't have to do this. I believe you.' Rachel: 'Thank you, Phoebe.' Phoebe (aside): 'But she didn't.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe publicly capitulates and says she believes Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's immediate aside — 'But she didn't' — is a deadpan breaking of the fourth wall that confirms she still doesn't believe Rachel while having just told her she does.
jokes.explanation: A clean, perfectly economical joke. The directness of Phoebe's aside — spoken in third person about herself — is funny and character-specific. 'But she didn't' is three words that completely undermine everything preceding them. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Check it out! I'm an ordained minister now. I can perform weddings!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And look — it's reversible! *flips jacket inside out* Now I'm ready to party!

jokes.text: Chandler finds something in the tux pocket. 'You carry that around?' The shop owner: 'I find it to be something of a conversation piece.' Chandler: 'Between you and...?' Owner: 'Gunther.'
jokes.setup: An unspecified object found in the tux pocket is a 'conversation piece.' The implication is it's something odd or inappropriate.
jokes.punchline: The only person the shop owner discusses it with is Gunther — the Central Perk barista who is chronically in love with Rachel. This is a perfect non-sequitur that characterizes both the owner as a marginal loner and ties him to the show's most pathetically lovesick character.
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly sharp joke. The build-up of 'conversation piece' implying something sophisticated is immediately deflated by Gunther's name — not because Gunther is dumb, but because Gunther is a background sad-sack character. The specificity of naming Gunther rather than a generic answer is what elevates this. Rewatch bonus for Gunther fans.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! You can't just leave! That's like, the only interesting thing that's ever happened to me!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not even mad about the kiss anymore, I just need you to admit it happened so I have something to tell people!

jokes.text: They try to put on both tuxes for a photo. Chandler: 'I would, but my pants are a little tight.' Ross: 'A little tight? I could see 00 and 7 in those things.'
jokes.setup: Chandler says his pants are 'a little tight' in the Bond tuxedo.
jokes.punchline: Ross's joke that you could see '00 and 7' in the tight pants — i.e., see the outline of his private parts labeled like a Bond code number — is a risqué visual wordplay joke.
jokes.explanation: A clever, slightly risqué wordplay joke. '00 and 7' as a genital reference within the Bond metaphor is creative and well-constructed. The pun works on multiple levels and the economy is excellent. Gets a bigger laugh than a standard groan-pun.

jokes.text: Chandler tries on the Batman jacket and exclaims: 'Holy double-vented comfort, Batman!'
jokes.setup: Chandler puts on the Batman tuxedo jacket for the first time.
jokes.punchline: He immediately delivers a 'Holy _____, Batman!' catchphrase from the 1960s TV show, substituting in 'double-vented comfort' — a tailoring term — for the usual exclamation.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed pop culture riff. The mashup of the Robin catchphrase with the specific tailoring term 'double-vented' is funny because it's unexpectedly specific. It's a character-specific Chandler joke too — he's the type to know tailoring terminology. Economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I kissed you?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It was very romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't remember that at all.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I do. And then we slow danced by the window, and you said you'd never felt this way before, and then we went to Paris.

jokes.text: They discover an invitation inside the pocket: the Val Kilmer tux was not from Batman — it was worn to the premiere of a romantic drama. Chandler reads: 'Val Kilmer didn't wear this in Batman. He wore it to the premiere of a fruity love story where he was a blind guy.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler have been fighting over and celebrating the Batman tux all episode.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that it was actually worn to a 'fruity love story' premiere (the film At First Sight) completely deflates the Batman cachet — and the description 'fruity love story where he was a blind guy' is Chandler's dismissive characterization.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural payoff to the Batman tux subplot. The deflation is well-earned after an episode of buildup. 'Fruity love story where he was a blind guy' is Chandler's voice perfectly — dismissive, slightly cruel, and very funny. The structure is excellent as a callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I kissed him and it was amazing. That proves I love him.

dialogue.speaker: Melissa
dialogue.line: No, it doesn't.

jokes.text: Ross: 'The only super power you have is the slightly heightened sense of smell.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just been deflated by the revelation that his tux is from a romantic drama, not Batman.
jokes.punchline: Ross twists the knife: the only 'super power' conferred by the blind-man premiere tux is 'slightly heightened sense of smell' — the compensatory ability blind people allegedly develop. Cruel, specific, and funny.
jokes.explanation: One of Ross's best lines in the episode. The logic is impeccable: blind man's tux → heightened sense of smell superpower → that's your Batman power now. The 'slightly' modifier is the perfect precision detail. Economical, original, and quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its cleverness.

jokes.text: Joey enters with his officiant robes. Monica immediately capitulates: 'I give up. Whatever you want, you can have it. You want to sing a song or do a dance? You want your mom at the altar screaming racial slurs? I don't care.'
jokes.setup: Joey has shown up in his flamboyant ceremony robes. Monica sees them.
jokes.punchline: Monica's reaction is an escalating series of surrenders — from 'whatever you want' to the increasingly extreme offers, culminating in 'your mom at the altar screaming racial slurs' — revealing her complete breakdown of standards.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Monica's complete psychological collapse from perfectionist wedding planner to 'I don't care if your mom screams racial slurs' is a magnificent escalation. Each offer is more extreme than the last. 'Racial slurs' is an unexpected dark turn that works because of the contrast with Monica's usual obsessive control. The escalation structure is excellent and very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Ehhh. You're like a B+.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A B+?!

jokes.text: I give up. Whatever you want, you can have it. You want to sing a song or do a dance? You want your mom at the altar screaming racial slurs? I don't care.
jokes.setup: Joey approaches Monica, apparently to negotiate again about the wedding. Monica pre-emptively surrenders.
jokes.punchline: She escalates from 'sing a song or do a dance' to 'your mom at the altar screaming racial slurs' — revealing how far Monica has mentally gone in imagining worst-case scenarios involving Joey's family.
jokes.explanation: Monica's total breakdown into 'I don't care' territory is funny, but the escalation to 'screaming racial slurs' is the real joke — both a callback to the Tribbianni family bigotry established earlier AND a perfect expression of how thoroughly Monica has been worn down. Dark but earned.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I finally found a tux that fits!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? How many stores did you have to go to?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, you know, just the usual... forty-seven.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Forty-seven?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I had to be thorough. I checked the return policies at all of them, tried on every tux in my size, and then I realized I was in the children's section for the first thirty.

jokes.text: Joey, missing Monica's distress entirely: 'I just want to thank you guys for what you did for my parents.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just had a complete meltdown about the robes. Joey has apparently not noticed any of this.
jokes.punchline: Joey's warm, sincere gratitude is completely disconnected from Monica's freak-out — he was talking about his parents the whole time, oblivious to her reaction.
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious sweetness is a reliable comedic beat. The contrast with Monica's hysteria is good, though the joke is mostly in the reaction rather than the words themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wow, Chandler, you look amazing! Where did you get that tuxedo?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks! I rented it from this place downtown.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it fits you perfectly. You look so sophisticated!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, there's just one thing...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's Oprah's.

jokes.text: Joey shows off how the robe converts: 'I wear it like this when I marry you guys. And then this... is for party time.'
jokes.setup: Joey is demonstrating his ceremony outfit. He shows the robe configuration for the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: The robe apparently has a 'party mode' — it converts into something more festive — and Joey's categorization of 'party time' as a distinct mode of his officiant outfit is delightfully absurd.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag. The convertible ceremony-to-party robe is a perfect Joey prop — he's planned the whole event as entertainment, complete with costume changes. 'Party time' as a distinct phase of the wedding is a great character detail. Relies heavily on the visual, which we can infer from context.

jokes.text: Rachel kisses Melissa to prove her point. Phoebe watches. After Melissa leaves declaring her love, Phoebe immediately kisses Rachel.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just kissed Melissa (dramatically, to prove the story) — and Melissa has responded by confessing she's in love with Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's immediate kiss of Rachel (after watching the whole exchange) is an impulsive decision to 'see what all the fuss is about' — revealing she's been curious this whole time.
jokes.explanation: A strong structural payoff. Phoebe's curiosity has been building all episode (her disbelief was always tinged with fascination). Her immediate impulse to try it herself after Melissa's big confession is the perfect Phoebe move — impulsive, curious, oblivious to social norms. The visual of her just going for it is what makes this land as a physical comedy beat.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'That night was the one wild thing I've ever done in my life. I won't let you take it away.'
jokes.setup: Melissa is denying the kiss and walking away.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's desperation is now fully exposed — she needs this story to be true for her own self-image. The comedy is in the gap between how Rachel sees herself (wild) and how everyone else sees her.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's vulnerability is both sympathetic and funny. The 'vanilla' callback lands here implicitly — she is exactly as vanilla as Monica said, and she knows it.

jokes.text: Melissa's confession: 'Of course I remember. I think about it all the time. I can still hear the coconuts knocking together... I didn't want to tell you, because I didn't think you'd return my love.'
jokes.setup: Melissa's denial has collapsed into a full romantic declaration.
jokes.punchline: The coconuts — a mundane detail from a college party — have apparently been haunting Melissa for years. The specificity of this detail ('I can still hear the coconuts') is delightfully absurd.
jokes.explanation: The coconuts becoming a romantic touchstone is a brilliant callback. What was a throwaway comic detail ('somewhere Joey's head is exploding') becomes the central image of Melissa's declaration. Well-structured payoff.

jokes.text: 'Look who's being suddenly shy.' — Phoebe to Rachel after Melissa's declaration.
jokes.setup: Rachel has kissed Melissa and triggered an unexpected declaration of love.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's dry observation that Rachel — who has been loudly insisting on this story — is now the shy one.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed reaction from Phoebe. The irony of Rachel's sudden shyness after all her insisting is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Melissa's rambling denial spiral: 'I'm not in love with you. I'm not in love with her. I don't hear coconuts banging together. I don't picture your face when I make love to my boyfriend.'
jokes.setup: Melissa tries to take back her declaration of love.
jokes.punchline: Each denial is more damning than the last — the final 'I don't picture your face when I make love to my boyfriend' is so specific that it completely confirms the opposite.
jokes.explanation: Melissa's denials escalating into the most self-incriminating possible statement is a brilliantly structured sequence. 'I don't picture your face when I make love to my boyfriend' would only be said by someone who absolutely does. The specificity makes it exceptional. The coconuts callback in the middle of the denial ('I don't hear coconuts banging together') is a perfect touch.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'What the hell was that?' Phoebe: 'Just wanted to see what all the fuss was about.' Rachel: 'And?' Phoebe: 'I've had better.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just kissed Rachel. Rachel demands an explanation.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's verdict — 'I've had better' — is a devastating flat review that simultaneously insults Rachel's kissing ability (the thing she just fought the whole episode to defend) and closes the loop on the main B-plot.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best button jokes in this era of Friends. The entire B-plot has been about Rachel desperately proving that the kiss happened AND that she's a good kisser. Melissa even said 'Nobody can kiss that good and not mean it.' Phoebe's flat 'I've had better' destroys ALL of that — Rachel's credential, her pride, and her victory — in three words. The economy is extraordinary (9.5), the structure is perfect (this is the ideal payoff to a 20-minute setup), and the character integration is excellent (only Phoebe would do this and deliver it this flatly). This is comparable to the 9.5 anchor in terms of structural perfection, though slightly less culturally iconic.

jokes.text: Chandler, after trying on many tuxedos, announces: 'I found one that fits.' Monica: 'Well, you know what they say? 23rd time's a charm.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has apparently tried on 22 tuxedos before finding one that fits.
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry riff on '3rd time's a charm' — expanding it to '23rd' — implies Chandler's body is so awkward that even renting a formal tux took 23 attempts.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean joke. The '23rd time's a charm' gag is a solid riff on a cliché. Character-specific to both Chandler's awkward physicality and Monica's dry wit. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Monica asks whose tux Chandler found. He hedges ('Does it matter?'). She insists. He finally: 'Diane Keaton.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has found a tux that fits him. Monica asks whose it is. He's suspiciously reluctant to say.
jokes.punchline: The tux belongs to Diane Keaton — a woman — which explains both why it fits Chandler's unusual proportions AND why he was embarrassed to say. The reveal also implies something about Diane Keaton's fashion choices (she's known for androgynous style) and Chandler's body.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed final joke that works on multiple levels. The misdirection (the hedging and reluctance) builds perfect anticipation. 'Diane Keaton' as the punchline works because: (1) she's a woman, (2) she's famous for androgynous menswear style (Annie Hall), (3) it implies Chandler has a woman's proportions. The structure — slow build, three rounds of asking, then the reveal — is textbook misdirection. Monica's silence is the button. This is the episode's closer and it sticks the landing. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

tmdb_overview: At Central Perk Rachel runs into her friend from college, Melissa, and it turns out they share something more than just a friendship. Meanwhile, Monica plans the seating arrangement for the wedding and is taken by surprise when Joey mentions that his parents are coming to the wedding too. Also, Chandler and Ross argue who gets to wear a celebrity tux for the event.
insight: Rachel kiss setup drowns in 58-point humor index; callbacks can't save weak episode.
